body.text: For much of the post-Cold War period, the US enjoyed a degree of dominance in West Asia unmatched by any other external power. The collapse of the Soviet Union left the US at the centre of the region’s security architecture, backed by military bases, alliances with Arab states, control over key diplomatic processes, and an increasingly close strategic partnership with Israel and Gulf States on a lower level. Even when American policies faced resistance, there was no comparable international power capable of challenging the US-led regional order as a whole.

That era is ending. The global system is moving towards greater multipolarity, and West Asia increasingly reflects that transformation. China has become a major economic and diplomatic actor; Russia has demonstrated its capacity to intervene in regional conflicts; and regional powers such as Iran, Türkiye, and Saudi Arabia have pursued increasingly autonomous foreign policies. Even traditional US partners have diversified their relationships rather than relying exclusively on the US. American power remains formidable, but its ability to organise the region unilaterally has diminished.

At its centre is Israel. Instead of maintaining regional primacy, primarily through extensive direct American involvement, the emerging model seeks to establish Israel as the dominant military, technological, and increasingly, economic power within a US-backed regional architecture. Arab states are encouraged to enter this order through the Abraham Accords and deeper economic, security, and technological integration with Israel. Those remaining outside it face a different form of pressure.

Seen from this perspective, the conflicts stretching from Gaza and southern Lebanon to Yemen, Iraq, and ultimately Iran are not entirely separate arenas. They form parts of a wider struggle over the forces capable of resisting an Israel-centred regional order. Hamas has been devastated and the Hezbollah severely weakened; pressure has intensified on Iran-aligned armed groups in Iraq and Yemen; and confrontation has increasingly moved towards Iran itself. The apparent objective is a West Asia in which no remaining regional actor possesses sufficient military capacity to seriously challenge Israeli superiority.

Trump’s grand strategy, therefore, is not simply about withdrawing America from West Asia. It seeks something more ambitious: American dominance with a smaller direct American footprint, with Israel functioning as the principal regional pillar of that order. The US would remain the ultimate guarantor, while Israel exercises an increasingly hegemonic role on the ground.

The question is whether such an order can endure. Military superiority can destroy capabilities, weaken adversaries, and compel governments to alter their behaviour. But regional orders require more than coercion. Trump’s strategy risks confusing the elimination of resistance with the creation of legitimacy, while underestimating the political and social forces that have repeatedly frustrated externally imposed projects in West Asia. The very attempt to establish a new hierarchy may ultimately generate the resistance that prevents it from becoming a stable order.
The end of the old American ‘Middle East’

The strategic environment Trump inherited was fundamentally different from the one the US dominated after the Cold War. With the Soviet Union gone, the US enjoyed an extraordinary degree of freedom of action across West Asia. The 1991 Gulf war (a US-led military campaign against Iraq after Saddam Hussein’s forces invaded and occupied Kuwait in August 1990, which eventually led to the expulsion of Iraqi forces from Kuwait in early 1991, reinforcing the US’ position as the dominant external military power in West Asia) demonstrated the extent of American military superiority. Security partnerships with Saudi Arabia and other Gulf monarchies, alliance with Israel, and a central role in Arab-Israeli diplomacy placed the US at the heart of the regional order. For much of the 1990s and early 2000s, no external power possessed either the capacity or the regional network to seriously compete with it.

The wars in Afghanistan and Iraq exposed the limits of this dominance. The US demonstrated that it could overthrow governments with remarkable speed, but also that converting military superiority into sustainable political orders was far more difficult. The costs of these interventions contributed to growing American reluctance to undertake large-scale military commitments, while the political consequences of the 2003 invasion of Iraq paradoxically created greater opportunities for Iran and its allies. They capitalised on the political and security vacuums that emerged as the US proved more successful at removing regimes than replacing them with functional and stable states. Iran and its allies gradually built a regional network that portrayed the US as a destabilising force and sought to reduce, and ultimately end, the American military presence in the region.

At the same time, the global balance of power was changing. Most importantly, China’s economic rise has given West Asia states an increasingly important alternative partner. This is particularly visible in the Gulf, where China has become the Gulf Cooperation Council’s (GCC) largest trading partner, according to a January 2025 report in Emirates News Agency WAM. In 2023, China accounted for 19.2 per cent of total GCC merchandise exports, worth $158.3 billion, and supplied 21.2 per cent of the GCC’s merchandise imports. By comparison, total US-GCC trade stood at approximately $93.6 billion that year, according to a May 2025 report in the Oman Daily Observer. The figures illustrate the extent to which the Gulf’s economic relationships have diversified beyond its traditional strategic dependence on the US.

The China-brokered restoration of Saudi-Iranian diplomatic relations in 2023 was particularly symbolic: two major regional states turned to China to facilitate an agreement concerning an issue at the heart of West Asian security.

Iran, meanwhile, developed a different form of power. Rather than competing with the US conventionally, Iran built networks of political and armed allies stretching through Iraq, Syria, and Lebanon to Yemen and the Palestinian territories. By investing on non-state actors, and anti-American and anti-Israeli sentiment, Iran established a regional sphere of influence that conventional US military superiority proved unable to eliminate for decades.

Perhaps more consequentially, America’s own partners have changed. Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Qatar, and Türkiye increasingly resist the idea that relations with the US require exclusive alignment with American geopolitical preferences. They maintain US security relationships while simultaneously developing economic ties with China, diplomatic channels with Iran, and, to varying degrees, relations with Russia. According to a February 2026 report in the Carnegie Politika, Russia has returned as a major player, and not just in Iran. Arab states increasingly reach out to Russia to create economic and security partnership.

The result is not the disappearance of American power. The US remains a powerful actor in the region. What has disappeared is the uncontested environment in which that power once operated. West Asia governments now have more partners, more alternatives, and consequently greater room to manoeuvre.

This is the geopolitical context in which Trump’s strategy should be understood. West Asia is participating in a wider transition from the unipolar moment of the post-Cold War era towards a more fragmented and multipolar international system. Trump’s response has not been to accommodate that transition smoothly.
Proxy hegemony

Trump’s emerging regional order appears to seek something different from the direct American hegemony that characterised post-Cold War West Asia. Rather than maintaining primacy primarily through extensive US military involvement, costly interventions, and continuous management of regional conflicts, the emerging model relies increasingly on Israel to enforce a favourable balance of power. In this sense, Trump is not abandoning American dominance but attempting to outsource a significant part of its regional enforcement to Israel.

This helps explain the extraordinary degree of political and military support that the US has extended to Israel. The objective can be understood as broader than defending an ally. Israel is being given greater strategic freedom to weaken the actors capable of challenging the emerging order, while the US provides the military supplies, diplomatic protection and, when necessary, direct military support that underpin its superiority. The result would be a division of labour: American power remains behind the regional order, but Israel increasingly acts as its principal military enforcer.

Iran is the main obstacle to such an arrangement because it has spent decades constructing an alternative network of power largely outside the US-led security architecture. Its relationships with the Hezbollah, Iraqi armed groups, the Houthis, and Palestinian factions gave Iran the capacity to pressure Israel and US partners from several directions without relying on conventional military superiority. Consequently, the confrontation with Iran cannot be understood solely through the nuclear issue. Weakening the wider “Axis of Resistance” is essential to removing the principal organised challenge to Israeli regional dominance.

The wars since October 2023 have dramatically advanced this process. Hamas’ military capabilities in Gaza have been severely degraded; the Hezbollah has been weakened through war and the loss of much of its senior leadership; the fall of Bashar al-Assad in Syria removed a crucial territorial link in Iran’s regional network; pressure has intensified on Iraqi armed factions to disarm or integrate fully into state institutions; the Houthis have faced sustained military attacks; and confrontation has ultimately reached Iran itself. Viewed separately, these developments have different local causes and dynamics. Viewed together, however, they have substantially weakened the network that previously constrained Israeli freedom of action across the region.

Iraq, Lebanon, and Syria are therefore particularly important to the emerging order. The US does not necessarily need these countries to become straightforward American allies. A more achievable objective is to strengthen central governments sufficiently to restrict autonomous armed actors and deny Iran the spaces through which it has historically projected power. In Lebanon, this means limiting the Hezbollah’s independent military capacity; in Iraq, bringing militia weapons under state control while drawing the country’s government economically and politically closer to the US and the Arab Gulf; and in post-Assad Syria, preventing the reconstruction of the Iranian military corridor that once connected Tehran to Lebanon.

The other side of the strategy is integration as a complement to coercion. The Abraham Accords provide the framework through which Arab states can be incorporated into an Israel-centred economic and security architecture. Normalisation potentially gives Israel not only diplomatic recognition but deeper access to regional markets, investment, technology partnerships, and security cooperation. Saudi participation would be the decisive prize: normalisation between the region’s largest Arab economy and Israel could transform the existing agreements into the foundation of a much broader regional arrangement.

Trump’s preferred method is therefore essentially two-track. States willing to join the emerging order are offered deals, investment, security partnerships, and closer relations with the US; actors capable of militarily resisting it face isolation, economic pressure, or force. His familiar sequence of threats, escalation, and overwhelming pressure followed by negotiation fits this model. The aim is to negotiate from a position in which the adversary’s alternatives have already been dramatically reduced.

This also explains an apparent contradiction in Trump’s approach. He wants the strategic benefits of American hegemony without returning to the occupations and nation-building that made US dominance increasingly costly. Israel provides a possible solution. Its military superiority allows the US to reduce its direct exposure while retaining a regional balance overwhelmingly favourable to American interests. The proposed transition is therefore not from American hegemony to American withdrawal, but from direct US hegemony towards an Israeli proxy hegemony backed by American power.
Weakness in the design

Yet the Iran war revealed the first major weakness in this design. The war has failed to achieve any of its goals. Iran still holds strong, and its allies, despite getting weakened, are still major player in Lebanon, Iraq, and Yemen. The Gulf states present another obstacle. Saudi Arabia, Qatar, and others may welcome American security guarantees and maintain close relations with the US, but they have also spent years expanding economic ties with China, engaging Russia, and reopening channels with Iran. They are increasingly pursuing strategic autonomy rather than exclusive alignment. The Makkah Joint Defence Agreement between Saudi Arabia, Pakistan, and Türkiye is a clear example of this trajectory. Trump’s project therefore asks regional states to enter a more hierarchical US-Israeli order at precisely the moment when many of them have acquired greater room to manoeuvre within an increasingly multipolar system.

That contradiction is central to assessing whether Trump’s strategy can succeed. Military power may clear the field of organised challengers, and economic incentives may attract governments into new arrangements, but neither necessarily creates a durable regional order. Trump is attempting to preserve American primacy while reducing the American burden of maintaining it. Whether Israel can exercise that delegated dominance without generating new forms of resistance is therefore not peripheral to the strategy—it is its central test.

Trump’s strategy has already demonstrated that the US and Israel possess the military and economic power to severely weaken individual adversaries and alter the regional balance. But weakening adversaries does not always lead to defeating them, and even defeating them is different from constructing a sustainable regional order. The more important question is whether military superiority can be translated into political legitimacy and lasting stability.

Modern West Asian history provides reasons for doubt. External powers have repeatedly succeeded in removing governments, destroying military capabilities, and changing balances of power, only to struggle with what followed. Iraq and Afghanistan are the clearest examples. The recurrent conflicts in Lebanon and Palestine also demonstrate the distance between military victory and durable political settlement. Coercion can change behaviour and destroy organisations; it cannot easily eliminate the political conditions that produced resistance in the first place.

This is particularly relevant to Iran. Weakening Iran and dismantling some of its regional network would undoubtedly transform the balance of power, but it would not automatically produce a pro-American or pro-Israeli West Asia. Iran’s influence did not emerge solely because it imposed itself on the region. It also grew from weak states, communal insecurity, unresolved conflicts, foreign interventions and, above all, the unresolved Palestinian question. Many of the movements aligned with Iran also possess local constituencies and political interests independent of Iran. Weakening their external patron may therefore not eliminate the resistance movement.

The proposed Israeli role creates an even deeper contradiction. Israel may become the strongest pillar of the new order while simultaneously becoming one of the principal sources of opposition to it. Its overwhelming military superiority can deter states and weaken armed groups, but regional hegemony requires more than the ability to impose costs. The devastation in Gaza and continuing Palestinian dispossession make it difficult to build political legitimacy for an order perceived by Arab publics as institutionalising Israeli dominance rather than resolving the conflict at its centre. Arab governments may cooperate with Israel for strategic reasons, but the greater the gap between state policy and public sentiment, the greater the domestic cost of that cooperation.

Moreover, the West Asia that Trump is attempting to reorganise is no longer the region that the US dominated in the 1990s. Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Türkiye, and other states increasingly pursue multi-alignment rather than exclusive partnerships. They can rely on American security cooperation while trading extensively with China, coordinating with Russia, negotiating with Iran and pursuing their own regional agendas. This is not simply global multipolarity reaching West Asia; it is multipolarity developing within the regional system itself. Washington may strengthen its partnerships, but restoring the hierarchical relationships of the unipolar era is a much more difficult proposition.

This exposes the fundamental contradiction in Trump’s grand strategy. The US wants weaker adversaries, Israeli military superiority, secure energy flows, constrained Chinese and Russian influence, and regional governments capable of controlling non-state armed actors. Yet, Trump simultaneously seeks to avoid prolonged occupations, expensive nation-building, large-scale permanent deployments and open-ended responsibility for regional stability. In effect, the US wants the political outcomes associated with hegemony without bearing the political, military and economic costs historically required to sustain it. Israel’s proxy hegemony is intended partly to resolve that contradiction, but it may instead reproduce it at another level.

Trump’s strategy may therefore deliver some tactical victories without producing the regional order it seeks. Iran can be weakened, armed groups can be degraded, governments can be pressured, and Israel’s military superiority can be expanded. But a durable order cannot be built through superiority alone. It requires political legitimacy, functioning institutions and settlements capable of addressing the conflicts from which resistance repeatedly emerges.

The irony is that Trump is attempting to preserve American primacy precisely when the international and regional systems are moving in the opposite direction. Replacing direct American hegemony with Israeli proxy hegemony may reduce the US’ immediate burden, but it does not resolve the fundamental problem: a multipolar West Asia is increasingly difficult for any single power—American, Israeli, or otherwise—to dominate.

Ali Mamouri is a research fellow at the Alfred Deakin Institute for Citizenship and Globalisation, Deakin University, Australia. He is the co-author of Diffusion of Digital Authoritarianism and a former Strategic Communications Adviser to the Iraqi Prime Minister and a former lecturer in the University of Sydney and the University of Tehran.
